 Delayed holiday flyers could benefit from deferred federal airline rule
 By Neal Augenstein 
 October 29, 2026 | 
 1:25 PM 
 | 
 Many air travelers whose flights are delayed or canceled this Thanksgiving and winter holiday season will remain eligible for compensation, after a recent delay in implementing a new U.S. Department of Transportation rule.
 Peter Greenberg, a travel journalist and analyst who writes at PeterGreenbergPro.com , tells WTOP that a law implemented under the Biden administration stated, “any time your plane was delayed or canceled for any other reason than weather, which is considered an act of God, you were due some compensation.”
 “So, if there was a mechanical delay and your plane was delayed, or maybe you were stranded, they got you a hotel room or they paid for a meal or alternate forms of transportation,” he said.
 But under the Trump administration, the Department of Transportation quietly rolled out the rule, “without holding any public hearings whatsoever,” Greenberg said, 
 The Department of Transportation rule excludes certain reasons for delays and cancellations from federal reporting requirements for airlines, including cyberattacks, the removal of an unruly passenger and aircraft damage from extreme weather. 
 “Unscheduled maintenance” is also on the list.
 “The rules would effectively give the airlines a ‘get out of jail free’ card on any mechanical delay, meaning that anything that was deemed unscheduled maintenance, they were not required to give you any kind of compensation at all,” Greenberg said.
 The rule was supposed to go into effect on Oct. 19. Two days before that, DOT pushed the effective date to Feb. 1, 2027.
 Greenberg said the new classification doesn’t make sense.
 “Everything is unscheduled maintenance,” he said. “If you have a flat tire, that’s unscheduled maintenance, but it’s still under your control. If the engine is leaking oil, that’s unscheduled maintenance, but it’s still under your control.”
 Greenberg said the DOT didn’t provide details on the reason for the delay, “except that it was requested by the airlines.”
 The bottom line? 
 “For the time being, if your flight is delayed or canceled for any other reason than weather, and it’s deemed under the airline’s operation control and responsibility, you are due some form of compensation,” he said.
 Other passenger protections remain in place 
 “The tarmac delay rule is still very much in effect,” Greenberg said. “If you’re pushing back from the gate, and the airline keeps you on the tarmac for any more than three hours, the airline is liable to a fine of up to $27,500 per passenger, so it’s in the airline’s best interest to get you back to the gate.”
 Looking long term, Greenberg guesses that the still-to-be-implemented rule will end up in litigation — perhaps filed by a passenger rights group — “because it gets the airlines off the hook for every conceivable delay or cancellation other than by cyberattack or by weather.”
 On Oct. 22, FlyersRights, the National Consumers League, the American Economic Liberties Project, Travelers United, and Consumer Action formally requested that DOT withdraw the rule, arguing it was issued in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act.
 “The rule sneakily transfers costs from airlines back to passengers for delays involving mechanical problems that are the responsibility and fault of airlines,” said Paul Hudson, president of FlyersRights, in a news release. “We are calling on the Department to withdraw the rule and proceed through lawful notice and comment rulemaking.”

 Fairfax Co. high schooler launches podcast to expose girls to careers in aviation industry
 By Scott Gelman 
 October 28, 2026 | 
 8:36 PM 
 | 
 Sanya Bhalla grew up about 10 minutes from Smithsonian's Udvar-Hazy Center in Chantilly, Virginia, and she was always fascinated by the large planes and space shuttles on display.
But she never fully envisioned flying one herself until she participated in the Smithsonian's She Can summer program as a 13-year-old. Through the program, Bhalla flew out of Manassas Regional Airport four times in a Cessna aircraft. She built and launched rockets and model airplanes. The group operated drones and visited Joint Base Andrews, where she observed an all-female C-17 crew.
The experience marked the first time Bhalla could picture herself pursuing a career in aviation.
Now a student at Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology, Bhalla is encouraging women to consider a career in aviation through her "She Flies Podcast," which launched in January 2026.
